objectives: Quantify NCD burden + describe MPOWER + FCTC + sugar tax evidence.
Apply behavioral models (HBM, TPB, TTM, nudges) to design interventions.
Choose between population-level + high-risk strategies (Geoffrey Rose) with worked examples.

slides.title: Non-communicable diseases + the big risk factors
slides.body:
**Non-communicable diseases (NCDs)** — cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory disease, diabetes — account for ~74% of global deaths (~41 million/yr; WHO 2024). Concentrated in middle-aged + working populations; rising fastest in LMICs (Atun + Khan; Bollyky; The Lancet NCDs Commission 2018 Bukhman + Mocumbi).

**Six leading modifiable risk factors** (WHO; GBD; Murray + Lopez):
- **Tobacco** — ~8 million deaths/yr globally; major cause of lung cancer, CVD, COPD, oral + esophageal + bladder cancers; ~1 in 4 cancer deaths. Doll + Hill (1954 British Doctors Study) + Surgeon General's Report 1964 (Luther Terry).
- **Hypertension** — ~10.8 million deaths/yr; leading single attributable risk factor.
- **Air pollution** — PM2.5 + ozone + household solid-fuel smoke — ~7 million deaths/yr.
- **Obesity + diet** — high BMI, low fruit + vegetables, high sodium, high sugar-sweetened beverages, processed meat — ~5 million+ deaths/yr.
- **Alcohol** — ~3 million deaths/yr; liver disease, road injuries, cancers.
- **Physical inactivity** — ~5 million premature deaths/yr.

**Framingham Heart Study** (1948-; NIH-funded longitudinal cohort of Framingham, Massachusetts) — discovered + quantified the modifiable cardiovascular risk factors (smoking, BP, cholesterol, diabetes, obesity) over 75+ years. Framingham Risk Score (Wilson + D'Agostino 1998) was the original 10-yr CVD risk calculator. SCORE2 (Europe), QRISK3 (UK), ASCVD pooled cohort (US) are modern descendants.

**Diabetes** — global prevalence ~537 million adults (IDF Diabetes Atlas 2024); doubling since 1980. Major driver of CKD, blindness, amputation, CVD. **Tom Friedan** (CDC director 2009-17) + WHO have emphasized diabetes as the bellwether NCD — a 21st-century epidemic driven by ultra-processed food + sedentary lifestyle.

**Cancer** — ~10 million deaths/yr (GLOBOCAN 2024 IARC). Top causes: lung, colorectal, liver, stomach, breast. Tobacco-attributable ~25-30%; HPV-attributable cervical + oropharyngeal ~5-8%; H. pylori-attributable gastric ~15%; alcohol-attributable ~5-7%. Increasing in LMICs from population growth + aging + risk-factor transitions.

**Chronic respiratory disease** — COPD ~3 million deaths/yr (mostly tobacco + occupational dust + biomass smoke); asthma ~250-400 million prevalence.

**Tobacco: MPOWER + WHO FCTC** — WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) 2003 was the first global health treaty (180+ parties). MPOWER package (2008):
- **M**onitor tobacco use + prevention policies.
- **P**rotect from smoke (smoke-free indoor laws).
- **O**ffer help to quit (cessation services, varenicline, bupropion, NRT).
- **W**arn about dangers (pictorial pack warnings, plain packaging — Australia 2012).
- **E**nforce bans on advertising, promotion, sponsorship.
- **R**aise taxes (10% real price increase → ~4-8% consumption fall; Jha + Chaloupka).

Global smoking prevalence among adults fell from ~33% (2000) to ~22% (2024); avoided millions of deaths. Plain packaging Australia 2012 (Cunningham; Wakefield 2015) → measurable consumption decline + 'gold standard' policy. Adoption now in UK, France, Ireland, Norway, NZ, Canada, Slovenia, Saudi Arabia.

**Alcohol policy** — WHO SAFER framework: **S**trengthen drink-driving laws; **A**dvance + enforce restrictions on availability; **F**acilitate screening + brief interventions; **E**nforce restrictions on marketing; **R**aise prices via taxes + minimum unit pricing. Minimum unit pricing Scotland (2018) → 13% reduction in alcohol-attributable mortality (Lewsey + Gallagher 2022 Lancet). Nordic alcohol monopolies (Vinmonopolet Norway; Systembolaget Sweden; Alko Finland) restrict availability + advertising; well-documented mortality reductions.

**Sugar tax + food policy** — Mexico 2014 1-peso/L sugar-sweetened beverage tax → 7.6% reduction in SSB purchases in first year (Colchero 2017 Lancet PH; cumulatively ~10% reduction). UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy (SDIL) 2018 — tiered tax drove ~50% reduction in sugar in soft drinks via reformulation (Pell + Hammond 2020 BMJ). Trans-fat ban UK + Denmark + WHO REPLACE program → CVD reductions (Restrepo + Rieger 2016).

slides.title: Behavioral models + nudges
slides.body:
**Health Behavior models** — frameworks for understanding why people adopt (or fail to adopt) health behaviors.

**Health Belief Model (HBM)** — Rosenstock + Hochbaum 1950s; **Victoria Champion** + Skinner refined Health Belief Model Scale. Predicts behavior change as a function of:
- **Perceived susceptibility** to disease.
- **Perceived severity** of disease.
- **Perceived benefits** of preventive action.
- **Perceived barriers** (cost, time, side effects).
- **Cues to action** (media, social).
- **Self-efficacy** (Bandura-derived).

Used for screening uptake, vaccination, condom use, mammography, COVID-19 NPI adherence.

**Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB)** — **Icek Ajzen** 1991. Behavior intention is a function of:
- **Attitudes** toward the behavior.
- **Subjective norms** (perceived social pressure).
- **Perceived behavioral control** (self-efficacy + actual control).

Intention → behavior; gap explained by perceived control + environment. Strong predictive validity in many domains.

**Transtheoretical Model (Stages of Change)** — **James Prochaska + DiClemente 1983**. Stages:
1. **Pre-contemplation** (not considering change).
2. **Contemplation** (considering within 6 mo).
3. **Preparation** (planning in next month).
4. **Action** (changed within last 6 mo).
5. **Maintenance** (sustained >6 mo).
6. (Termination.)

Intervention should match stage: motivational interviewing (contemplation), behavioral skills + supports (action), relapse prevention (maintenance). Widely used in smoking cessation, weight loss, addiction.

**Social Cognitive Theory** — Bandura 1986. Self-efficacy + observational learning + reciprocal determinism.

**Behavioral Insights + nudges** — **Richard Thaler + Cass Sunstein** 'Nudge' (2008; Thaler Nobel 2017). Behavior is shaped by 'choice architecture'; small changes in defaults, framing, salience, social norms can produce large changes without restricting choice (libertarian paternalism).

**Behavioral Insights Team (BIT)** — 'Nudge Unit' founded UK 2010 under **David Halpern**; spun out 2014 + privatized. Replicated globally (US Office of Evaluation Sciences, EU JRC, Australia BETA, OECD). Major findings + applications:
- **Defaults**: organ-donation opt-out (Spain, France, UK) → 80-100% donor rates vs ~15% opt-in (US, Germany before law). Pension auto-enrollment.
- **Social norms**: 'Most people pay taxes on time' → tax compliance increase 5-15% (UK HMRC trials).
- **Framing**: 'gain' vs 'loss' framing in health messaging; positive framing for prevention, loss framing for screening (Rothman + Salovey).
- **Salience + simplification**: redesigned forms, plain-language reminders, SMS prompts → vaccination uptake, screening attendance.
- **Commitment devices**: smoking-cessation deposits forfeited if relapse (Volpp + Loewenstein); savings for HbA1c targets.
- **Choice architecture in food**: cafeteria placement of healthy foods; default portion sizes; menu calorie labels (Bleich + Wolfson).

**Successes + limits of nudge**:
- Strong evidence for defaults, reminders, social norms.
- Modest effect sizes (often 1-5 percentage points).
- Less effective for highly addictive behaviors (smoking, alcohol, opioid) where structural + price interventions dominate (Marteau; Adams + White 2016 BMJ — 'Why nudging is not enough').
- Equity concerns: nudges may benefit advantaged groups more.
- Ethical critique: paternalism + manipulation (debated by Sunstein himself).

**Implementation science** — bridging research → practice. Frameworks: CFIR (Damschroder), RE-AIM (Glasgow), EPIS (Aarons). Critical for scaling NCD interventions in real-world health systems.

slides.title: Geoffrey Rose: population vs high-risk strategies
slides.body:
**Geoffrey Rose** (1926-1993; LSHTM) — 'Sick Individuals and Sick Populations' BMJ 1985; 'The Strategy of Preventive Medicine' (1992 book; reissued 2008). The most influential single framing in modern public health.

**Rose's core insight**: the determinants of why an individual gets sick differ from determinants of why the population has the rate it does. Two distinct strategies for prevention:

**1. High-risk strategy** — identify individuals at high risk + treat / counsel them.
Examples: statin therapy for high LDL, BP medications for hypertension, intensive lifestyle counseling for prediabetes (DPP), screening + treatment for high cholesterol.
Advantages: high motivation (patient + clinician), efficient per-person, large personal benefit, ethically uncontroversial.
Disadvantages: misses the majority of cases (which arise from the moderate-risk middle of the distribution); palliative (doesn't address upstream causes); costly screening + treatment + adherence; widens disparities (advantaged groups comply more).

**2. Population strategy** — shift the whole distribution.
Examples: salt reduction in food supply (UK 2003-11 voluntary reformulation reduced mean SBP ~3 mmHg → ~9000 fewer CVD deaths/yr); sugar tax; tobacco price + advertising bans; trans-fat ban; water fluoridation; folic acid food fortification; plain-packaging tobacco; food-labeling.
Advantages: targets the majority of cases (from the moderate middle); addresses upstream causes; equitable (reaches everyone); sustainable (often once-and-done policy); cost-effective.
Disadvantages: small per-person benefit (prevention paradox); political resistance from industry; less visible 'wins' for clinicians + patients; requires intersectoral action (taxation, agriculture, urban planning, trade).

**Rose's three insights**:
1. **Population mean predicts the tail.** A population's BP, cholesterol, alcohol, BMI distribution shift together; intervening on the mean shifts the tail too. (Ledermann's distribution for alcohol.)
2. **Large numbers at low risk produce more cases than small numbers at high risk.** Sums dominate.
3. **Causes of cases vs causes of incidence.** Why does *this person* have the disease (individual) vs why does *this population* have a certain rate (environmental + structural).

**Tobacco control as the canonical population win**:
- **Price** — tobacco taxes (~10% real price increase → ~4-8% consumption reduction; Jha 2014; Chaloupka). Most cost-effective single intervention.
- **Smoke-free workplaces** + restaurants + bars (Ireland 2004 first; CHF + AMI reductions Sargent + Glantz; Hamlyn 2007 Helena Montana study).
- **Plain packaging** (Australia 2012); pictorial warnings.
- **Advertising + sponsorship bans**.
- **Cessation services + NRT + varenicline + bupropion.**
- **MPOWER + FCTC** consolidate evidence + policy.
- Result: US adult smoking prevalence fell from ~42% (1965) to ~12% (2024). Avoided millions of premature deaths.

**Sugar tax + food policy** — Mexico (2014; 1-peso/L SSB tax → 7.6% first-year drop; ~10% cumulative; Colchero); UK SDIL (2018; tiered tax drove ~50% reformulation; Pell + Hammond 2020 BMJ); Chile (2016; mandatory front-of-pack warnings on high-sugar + sodium + saturated fat → 24% drop in sugary drinks; Taillie 2020). Mounting evidence for fiscal + labeling interventions.

**Nordic alcohol monopoly model** — Vinmonopolet (Norway), Systembolaget (Sweden), Alko (Finland) — government monopoly on retail alcohol sales restricts hours, advertising, density. Compared to fully privatized markets (e.g., Iceland 1989; British Columbia 2003 partial), monopoly settings show ~10-30% lower alcohol-attributable mortality (Babor; Norström + Ramstedt). Scotland minimum unit pricing 2018 (£0.50/unit) → 13% reduction in alcohol-attributable mortality (Wyper + Stockwell 2023 Lancet PH).

**UK trans-fat ban** — voluntary reformulation 2007-2010 (Restrepo + Rieger 2016); estimated >3000 CHD deaths averted/yr. WHO REPLACE 2018 targets global trans-fat elimination by 2023 (Hyseni + Capewell).

question.question: Apply Stages of Change + nudges to a smoking-cessation program
question.goal: A national smoking-cessation program serves 100,000 smokers/yr. Pre-contemplation 40%, contemplation 30%, preparation 15%, action 10%, maintenance 5%. Design interventions matched to stage.

steps.prompt: What intervention best fits pre-contemplation (40,000 smokers)?
steps.reveal: Pre-contemplators are not considering change. Best leverage: structural (price increases, smoke-free laws, plain packaging, pictorial warnings, mass-media counter-marketing). These work without requiring individual readiness. Tobacco-control history: large price + advertising-ban effects on this group; nudges have modest effect.

acceptedAnswers: motivational interviewing + personalized risk information + nudges to quit lines

steps.reveal: Contemplators are ambivalent. Use motivational interviewing (Miller + Rollnick) + personalized risk + benefit messages (HBM-aligned), reminders to quit-lines + apps (text2quit, NHS Smokefree), nudges: 'Most people in your neighborhood are quitting.' Brief interventions in primary care + by pharmacists are highly cost-effective.

acceptedAnswers: quit-date setting + NRT + varenicline + behavioral counseling + commitment devices

steps.reveal: Prepare smokers to quit: set a quit date, prescribe NRT or varenicline or bupropion (combo + counseling ~30% 12-mo abstinence; Cahill 2013 Cochrane), arrange behavioral support (group or individual), recommend commitment devices (financial pledges Volpp + Loewenstein), peer support, identify triggers + coping. Default opt-in cessation referral at point of care.

Action + Maintenance: regular follow-up (1 wk + 1 mo + 3 mo + 6 mo + 12 mo); SMS check-ins; manage withdrawal + cravings (extended NRT, varenicline 24 wk regimen); identify high-risk situations + plan responses; involve social support; congratulate small wins + reinforce identity ('I'm a non-smoker'). Reduce environmental cues (avoid smoking spaces, dispose of paraphernalia). ~50% relapse in first 12 mo; persistent attention needed.

steps.prompt: Apply Rose: what additional population-level interventions complement these stage-matched approaches?

acceptedAnswers: tax + price + advertising bans + smoke-free policies + plain packaging + cessation default

steps.reveal: Population strategy multiplies cessation gains: tax increases (10% real → 4-8% consumption fall; affects all stages, especially pre-contemplators), plain packaging + warnings, smoke-free laws (Ireland 2004, ~13% AMI reduction), advertising + sponsorship bans, default referral to cessation services at every clinical encounter, age-21 (Tobacco-21 US 2019). Combined with individual stage-matched services, drives a virtuous cycle: shrinks pre-contemplation pool by making smoking unaffordable + visible-bad + restricted; increases preparation + action; supports maintenance via environment.

question.question: Why does Mexico's 2014 sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) tax illustrate Rose's population strategy + the limits of pure nudge-based approaches?
options: Mexico's 1-peso/L SSB tax (~10% price increase) drove a 7.6% drop in SSB purchases in year 1 (Colchero 2017 Lancet PH) + ~10% cumulatively. It is a *population* intervention — shifts the whole distribution of sugar intake, regardless of stage of change or motivation, without requiring individual behavior change. By contrast, nudges (default soda sizes, calorie labels) yield 1-3% behavior shifts. Rose's prevention paradox applies: per-person benefit is small + invisible, but aggregated across ~130 million Mexicans the population health benefit is substantial. Fiscal + structural interventions complement behavioral models; pure nudge cannot reach the upstream price + supply.
question.explanation:
**Mexico SSB tax (2014)** — 1-peso/L excise on sugar-sweetened beverages. Colchero (Lancet PH 2017): 7.6% reduction in SSB purchases first year, falling further to ~10% cumulative; greater reduction among lowest-SES households. Equivalent reductions in calorie + sugar intake. Estimated long-term benefits: reductions in BMI, T2DM incidence, CVD (Sánchez-Romero 2016 PLoS Med modeled ~189k DALYs averted over 10 yr).

**Population vs nudge**: nudges (calorie labels, traffic-light food labels, default smaller portions) yield small effects (1-3% behavior change). Taxes + structural interventions shift the population, regardless of individual stage of change. Critique of pure nudge (Marteau 2011; Adams + White 2016 BMJ): nudge cannot reach the upstream price + supply + advertising determinants; fiscal + regulatory interventions are required for large effects. **Rose's population strategy** + nudges are complements, not substitutes.

hints: What shifts the population distribution of sugar intake?
Compare a 10% tax effect to a calorie-label nudge.
slides.workedSolution: Mexico's SSB tax drove ~7.6% drop in purchases year 1 (Colchero 2017 Lancet PH), with larger effect in low-SES groups. Population strategy shifts the whole distribution; pure nudges (labels, defaults) yield 1-3% changes. Fiscal + structural interventions reach upstream price + supply that nudges cannot.

question.question: Designing a national salt-reduction strategy
question.prompt: Your country has mean adult sodium intake ~10 g/d (WHO target <5 g/d). 80% of dietary sodium comes from processed food + restaurants, not table salt. CVD is the leading cause of death + lower-SES groups have 2× the stroke rate. You have a 5-year horizon + medium political will. Design a strategy that: (a) combines Rose's population approach with high-risk approaches (BP screening + medication); (b) uses voluntary then mandatory food-industry reformulation (UK FSA model 2003-11 vs Argentina mandatory 2013); (c) leverages behavioral insights (front-of-pack warning labels Chile 2016, traffic-light UK, Nutri-Score France); (d) addresses food-industry political-economy obstacles; (e) sets monitoring indicators (mean SBP, mean urinary sodium via spot samples, food sodium content via Action on Salt sampling); (f) projects population CVD reduction (each 1 g salt reduction → ~3 mmHg SBP → ~5-8% stroke reduction); (g) addresses equity gap (front-of-pack labels favor lower-literacy populations, taxes can be regressive); (h) describes the intersectoral collaboration (Ministries of Agriculture, Trade, Finance, Education) needed.

question.question: A 10% real price increase on tobacco reduces cigarette consumption by ~5%. A country has 5 million smokers + a baseline of 50,000 tobacco-attributable deaths/yr. The government implements a 20% real-tax-driven price increase, and consumption falls accordingly. Roughly how many tobacco-attributable deaths are averted/yr at new steady state, assuming linear relationship between consumption + mortality?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how Geoffrey Rose's population vs high-risk distinction + Thaler-Sunstein's nudge framework are complementary (not competing) for NCD prevention.
question.rubric: Mentions: Rose's population strategy shifts the mean of risk-factor distributions via structural interventions (tobacco taxes + plain packaging + smoke-free; salt reformulation; sugar tax; trans-fat ban; urban walkability); high-risk strategy treats individuals at clinical thresholds (statins, antihypertensives, GLP-1, intensive lifestyle); nudges (Thaler + Sunstein; UK BIT under Halpern) reshape choice architecture (defaults, reminders, social norms, salience) for modest individual-level shifts. Population strategy reaches the moderate majority + drives largest aggregate benefit (Rose's prevention paradox); high-risk strategy provides large per-person benefit + ethical 'rescue'; nudges complement both — e.g., default opt-out organ donation, auto-enrollment in pension, SMS reminders for screening + vaccination. Conclude: optimal NCD strategy combines all three layers — structural + clinical + nudge — coordinated intersectorally.
